skills.name: Font Pairing & Selection
skills.summary: Choosing type families that work together: contrast strategies, superfamily and companion approaches, licensing, and fallback stacks.

sections.definition: Font pairing is the deliberate selection of two (at most three) type families whose contrast creates hierarchy without visual conflict: a display face for headlines, a text face for reading, optionally a mono for code and data. The pairing decision compounds through every screen, so it is made once with explicit criteria - x-height compatibility, width contrast, tone match, license cost, and language coverage - rather than by browsing font sites until something looks nice.
principles: Maximum two families in the product: a superfamily (same designer, built to pair) or a display+text combo; a third slot is reserved for mono/code.
Pair by contrast, not similarity: pick faces that differ in one strong axis (serif vs sans, geometric vs humanist) - two similar-but-not-identical sans faces look like a mistake.
Match x-heights within ~5%: paired faces set side by side read as the same size only when x-heights agree.
Tone must match the brand: a quirky display face cannot rescue a legal document; tone-fit is checked against the brand's voice before aesthetics.
Check language coverage before falling in love: Vietnamese needs stacked-diacritic support (font-pairing meets multilingual-vietnamese here).
Verify license scope: webfont license, app embedding, and modification rights differ per foundry - budget the license with the token (design-tokens guide 02).
Every selection ships with a fallback stack: system fonts that keep metrics close so FOUT and font failures degrade gracefully.

tokens.notes: The documented strategy: superfamily | display+text | mono-add-on
Must cover all product locales before adoption

composition: Composes with type-scale (guide 02): the pairing defines families; the scale defines sizes - a family swap must not change the scale.
Composes with skill-design-tokens guide 02: pairing decisions land as typography tokens with fallback stacks and weight budgets.
Composes with styleAffinity: the pairing is the strongest single carrier of design style - it is chosen against the skill-ui-ux style direction.
patterns: Pairing scorecard: candidates rated on contrast axis, x-height match, tone fit, license cost, language coverage, and performance before adoption.
Superfamily shortcut: when in doubt, pick a superfamily (built-in pair) and spend the saved effort on scale and rhythm instead.
useCases: New products choosing their type system from scratch.
Rebrands evaluating whether to keep or replace the text face.
Localizing products into Vietnamese or other diacritic-heavy scripts.
antiPatterns: Font-of-the-week: swapping families per campaign until no one recognizes the product's voice
Twins pairing: two geometric sans faces at 92% similarity that read as an accident
Unlicensed embedding: shipping desktop-licensed fonts as webfonts
Fallback-less stacks: custom faces with no metric-matched system fallback, so failures reflow the page

accessibility.notes: Pairing serves accessibility directly: adequate x-height, open apertures, and unambiguous letterforms (I/l/1, O/0) reduce reading errors - and language coverage is an inclusion decision, not a nice-to-have.
accessibility.fallback: If a preferred face lacks Vietnamese coverage, the fallback face takes the whole product rather than mixing per-locale - mixed systems break rhythm.

skills.name: Modular Type Scale
skills.summary: A root-16px modular scale (ratio ~1.25) that covers body through display in 9 steps - hierarchy by stepping, never by improvising.

sections.definition: A modular type scale is a geometric progression of font sizes built from one base (16px) and one ratio (~1.25 major third): 16, 20, 25, 31, 39, 49... A closed scale means every hierarchy decision is 'step up or down' - never invent 17px or 22px. The scale is the contract between design and code: type tokens (skill-design-tokens guide 02) express it, and every text class steps along it.
principles: Root 16px, ratio 1.2-1.25: 1.25 (major third) suits most products; 1.2 for dense UI, 1.333 for dramatic marketing.
9 steps cover everything: body sits at step 0-1; display at 6-8 - if a design needs step 12, the ratio is wrong, not the count.
Size steps imply weight pairing: each step ships with its weight and line-height as a bundle, never a naked size.
Smallest legible step is 12px: below 12px, detail loss and x-height collapse hurt readability - captions floor here.
Scale in rem: steps multiply with user font-size preferences (WCAG 1.4.4).
Display sizes get negative tracking: as size grows, letter-spacing tightens (-0.01 to -0.03em) - see letter-spacing guide.
One scale for the whole product: marketing pages may extend upward, never sideways into a second parallel scale.
composition: The scale feeds typography tokens (skill-design-tokens guide 02): sizes are rem values with paired weights and line-heights.
It composes with fluid-responsive: heading steps interpolate via clamp() between two scale stops - the scale defines the stops.
It composes with spacing tokens: vertical rhythm snaps text blocks to the 4px grid via line-height + space tokens.
patterns: Named text roles: .text-body/.text-heading/.text-display bundle (size, weight, line-height, tracking) - consumers pick roles, not sizes.
Step-up hierarchy check: any screen where hierarchy needs more than 3 consecutive steps is restructured, not re-scaled.
useCases: Design systems defining their type ramp (the scale IS the ramp).
Auditing for off-scale sizes: every 17px/22px found is a token violation.
Marketing vs product: extending the same scale upward for display rather than forking scales.
antiPatterns: Off-scale sizes: 17px and 22px one-offs that quietly dissolve the scale
Ratio perfectionism: forcing 1.618 everywhere and getting display sizes too big for real UI
Naked sizes: shipping size tokens without weight/line-height pairing - hierarchy fragments
Parallel scales: product and marketing type systems that share nothing and drift forever

accessibility.notes: A rem-based scale is the WCAG 1.4.4 guarantee: the whole hierarchy multiplies with user font-size settings; the 12px floor keeps small text legible.
accessibility.fallback: If a display step overflows containers at 200% zoom, allow wrapping (never shrink the step) and check the fluid-responsive clamp bounds.

skills.name: Line-Height & Rhythm
skills.summary: Leading inversely proportional to size: 1.1-1.2 display, 1.5 body, 1.7 long-form - plus the vertical rhythm that aligns text to the 4px grid.

sections.definition: Line-height (leading) controls reading comfort and vertical rhythm: tight for display (1.1-1.2), relaxed for body (1.5), looser for long-form (1.7). It is the quietest typography decision - nobody notices good leading, everybody feels bad leading - and in Vietnamese and other stacked-diacritic scripts, line-height is also the difference between readable and clipped text.
principles: Line-height decreases as size increases: display 1.1-1.2, headings 1.2-1.3, body 1.5, long-form 1.7.
Unitless line-heights only: unitless values inherit as ratios and scale with font size - px line-heights break at every zoom level.
Body line-height never below 1.5: WCAG 1.4.12 users and dyslexic readers need the air; 1.5 is the floor for paragraphs.
Diacritics need headroom: Vietnamese stacked marks (ề, ậ) require line-height >= 1.5 and fallbacks that do not clip - verify at every step.
Rhythm comes from line-height + spacing tokens: paragraph spacing uses space tokens; the combination snaps text to the 4px grid.
Headings snap into rhythm: round heading line-height boxes to grid multiples where layout alignment matters.
CJK and Latin differ: CJK runs taller (1.7-2.0); locale-aware line-height tokens prevent cramped mixed-script text.

tokens.notes: h1-h4; tight but safe for diacritics at 2xl+
Buttons, list items, labels - compact but uncramped
Paragraph spacing from the 4px grid, not margin guesses
Vertical rhythm snaps to the spacing scale
CJK locale variant; taller boxes for dense glyphs
Vietnamese stacked marks never clip below 1.5

composition: Composes with type-scale: every scale step ships with its line-height as a bundle - the pair is reviewed together.
Composes with spacing tokens (skill-design-tokens guide 03): rhythm = line-height boxes + space tokens; margins are typographic exceptions only.
Composes with multilingual-vietnamese: diacritic headroom is a hard constraint that can override aesthetic tightness.
patterns: Role-bundled leading: text roles bundle (size, weight, line-height, tracking) so no consumer invents a leading value.
Grid-snapped headings: headings get line-height computed so their box lands on the 4px grid, aligning section starts.
useCases: Long-form reading products (docs, news) tuning 1.5-1.8 for comfort.
Vietnamese/cedilla-heavy locales verifying no clipped marks at any size.
Design systems enforcing unitless leading and grid rhythm.
antiPatterns: Px line-heights: fixed leading that clips at zoom and breaks user font scaling
One leading everywhere: 1.5 display type (loose, limp) or 1.2 body (cramped, exhausting)
Clipped diacritics: 1.15 line-height on Vietnamese headings shearing ề and ậ marks
Margin chaos: paragraph spacing invented per component instead of grid-snapped space tokens

accessibility.notes: Unitless leading is the WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.12 guarantee: text scales with user settings and layouts tolerate user spacing overrides; the 1.5 body floor serves dyslexic and low-vision readers.
accessibility.fallback: If tight display leading clips diacritics, raise that step's line-height - aesthetics yield to legibility every time.

skills.name: Letter-Spacing & Tracking
skills.summary: Tracking that tightens with size and loosens for uppercase: the micro-typography that makes headlines breathe and labels read.

sections.definition: Letter-spacing (tracking) adjusts the space between characters: display sizes need negative tracking (large glyphs carry their own air), uppercase labels need positive tracking (+0.04-0.08em) to separate uniform-height letters, and body text stays at 0. It is the smallest typographic token with an outsized effect - good tracking makes headlines look typeset, bad tracking makes them look broken.
principles: Track inversely to size: display -0.02 to -0.04em, headings -0.01 to -0.02em, body 0, small caps/labels +0.04 to +0.08em.
Never letter-space lowercase body: tracking body text destroys letterform recognition and reading speed - it is for display and labels only.
Uppercase earns its tracking: ALL-CAPS text without +0.04em reads as a dense wall; the tracking IS the readability.
Bold + tight is the display pairing: heavy weights at large sizes with -0.02em tracking is the modern headline look.
Tracking in em, not px: em-based values scale with font size and survive zoom and fluid type.
Pairs with the face's design: some families ship with optical tracking built in (SF Pro, Inter display cuts) - do not double-track.
Arabic/Indic scripts never track: connected scripts break when letter-spaced; tracking tokens apply to Latin/CJK display only.

tokens.notes: Uppercase overlines, nav labels, table headers
Uppercase buttons get minimal air; lowercase buttons stay 0
Never tighter; ligature and kerning collisions begin
Connected scripts exempt from all tracking
Prefer optical size axes/Display cuts over manual tracking
Tracking ships bundled in text roles, never standalone

composition: Composes with type-scale: tracking values bundle into the scale's text roles (size + weight + tracking are one decision).
Composes with uppercase patterns in component design (skill-component-recipes): table headers, badges, and eyebrows consume tracking-label/microcopy.
Composes with variable-fonts: optical size axes may replace manual tracking - the token records which strategy the family uses.
patterns: Bundled text roles: tracking never appears as an inline style; it lives inside .text-display/.text-label role definitions.
Uppercase checklist: any ALL-CAPS style must ship with tracking >= 0.04em and a lint rule - uppercase-without-tracking is the classic failure.
useCases: Marketing headlines and hero sections (negative tracking on display).
Dense enterprise UI: uppercase table headers and nav labels that stay readable.
Auditing micro-typography: tracked-out body text and untracked caps walls.
antiPatterns: Tracked-out body: +0.1em on paragraphs - slower reading, worse recognition, zero benefit
Untracked caps walls: ALL-CAPS labels at 0 tracking reading as dense blocks
Px tracking: fixed values that break at zoom and fluid sizes
Tracking connected scripts: letter-spacing on Arabic/Indic/Thai that severs the joins

accessibility.notes: WCAG 1.4.12 protects the user's right to override spacing: tracking tokens must not fight user stylesheets, and body tracking of 0 is the default the override assumes.
accessibility.fallback: If a display face needs extreme tracking for the brand, apply it only above the reading-size threshold - reading text keeps user-controllable default spacing.

skills.name: Typographic Hierarchy
skills.summary: Directing the eye with size, weight, color, and position - the four hierarchy levers applied through text roles instead of per-screen decoration.

sections.definition: Typographic hierarchy is the deliberate ranking of text so users parse a page's structure in milliseconds: what is the title, what supports it, what is meta. It is built from four levers - size (strongest), weight, color, and position - applied sparingly through a closed set of text roles. Pages with clear hierarchy scan well; pages without it force users to read everything to find anything.
principles: Size is the strongest lever: one 2x step says more than any weight change - use it for the single primary element per view.
Weight before color: bold/semibold creates hierarchy without leaving the accessible color set - color changes must still pass contrast.
Color ranks last and passes contrast: secondary text gets its own validated alias (design-tokens guide 05), not an arbitrary gray.
One focal point per screen: exactly one element gets the strongest treatment; two competing 'tops' read as none.
Three to four levels per screen: title / heading / body / meta - more levels fragment into noise.
Hierarchy is consistent across screens: the same role means the same rank everywhere (governance enforces it).
Position and grouping support, not replace, type: proximity and alignment from the layout system back up the type hierarchy.

tokens.notes: title / heading / body / meta per screen
Page title; the single focal rank
Bold before color before size for inline emphasis
Exactly one strongest treatment per screen
De-ranking text uses the validated secondary alias
Title vs body differs by >= 2 scale steps to register
Same role = same rank everywhere; lint-checked

composition: Hierarchy consumes the type-scale roles and validated color aliases - it is the application layer of both.
It composes with skill-ui-ux styles: each style weights the levers differently (minimalism: size+space; maximalism: size+color).
It composes with skill-design-review guide 02: the hierarchy audit applies this guide's rules as its checklist.
patterns: Role-mapping session: for each screen type, map every text element to one of the 4 roles before styling - orphan elements become decisions, not defaults.
Squint test: blur the screen; if the structure is invisible, hierarchy failed - fix levers, not pixels.
useCases: Landing pages where the eye must land on one thing first.
Dense dashboards ranking KPIs, labels, and meta consistently.
Documentation: title/heading/body/meta roles across thousands of pages.
antiPatterns: Everything emphasized: bold + color + size everywhere leaves nothing emphasized
Gray-on-gray de-ranking: secondary text below 4.5:1 to 'de-emphasize' (fails 1.4.3)
Five-plus levels: hierarchy fragments into noise when every element gets its own treatment
Per-screen improvisation: inventing hierarchy styles per page instead of consuming shared roles

accessibility.notes: Hierarchy must survive without color (1.4.1) and pass contrast at every rank (1.4.3): heading structure (h1-h6) also IS the screen reader's map (see a11y repo nav-by-headings).
accessibility.fallback: If visual hierarchy and semantic heading structure conflict, semantic wins - restyle the visuals to match the outline.

skills.name: Fluid & Responsive Typography
skills.summary: clamp()-interpolated type that scales with the viewport between scale stops - smooth scaling without breakpoint soup.

sections.definition: Fluid typography interpolates font sizes continuously with the viewport width using clamp(min, fluid, max): text grows smoothly between two scale stops instead of jumping at breakpoints. Applied to heading roles (not body - body stays fixed at readable sizes), it eliminates the 'title looks huge on mobile / timid on desktop' problem while keeping every size anchored to the modular scale.
principles: Fluid applies to headings, not body: body text is already optimal at 16-18px; fluid body drifts into unreadable territory.
clamp() between two scale stops: clamp(1.563rem, calc(1.2rem + 2vw), 3.052rem) - the endpoints ARE scale steps, nothing off-scale renders.
Compute the vw coefficient deliberately: slope = (max - min) / (viewportMax - viewportMin); hand-tuned vw values break the scale.
Cap the growth: the max clamp bound exists so 4K screens do not render 200px titles.
Test the extremes: 320px and 2560px are the design targets, not 1440px alone.
Line-height rebalances at extremes: tight display leading may need a higher value at min sizes - use clamp on line-height too when needed.
Access the user preference: fluid type still multiplies with root font-size (rem-based) - WCAG 1.4.4 holds at every viewport.

tokens.notes: Body exempt from fluidity by policy
Display leading loosens at small sizes
No interpolated value ever renders below 12px
Clamp endpoints must be modular-scale steps

composition: Fluid typography consumes the modular scale's stops as clamp endpoints - fluidity never introduces off-scale sizes.
It composes with responsive-layout (skill-responsive-layout guides 01-03): type fluidity is one axis of the layout system's responsiveness.
It composes with accessible-typography: rem-based clamps preserve zoom and user-preference scaling (WCAG 1.4.4).
patterns: Fluid role set: only the heading roles (h1-h3) get fluid tokens; every other text role stays at fixed scale steps - simplicity by exclusion.
Slope-per-step: precompute the vw slope per step for the documented viewport range; the formula lives beside the tokens.
useCases: Marketing sites: hero titles that fill space gracefully from phone to desktop.
Docs platforms: consistent headings across any viewport without breakpoints.
Audit: finding hand-tuned vw sizes whose endpoints are off-scale.
antiPatterns: Fluid body text: paragraphs shrinking to 13px on phones because everything interpolated
Unbounded vw: text-[5vw] growing forever on 4K displays
Off-scale endpoints: clamp bounds that are not scale steps, quietly forking the ramp
Fluid-only testing: signing off at 1440px while 320px renders cramped or 2560px renders cartoonish

accessibility.notes: rem-based clamps are the trick that keeps fluid type accessible: values multiply with root font-size, so WCAG 1.4.4 and user preferences hold at every viewport width.
accessibility.fallback: If a user override at 200% zoom collides with fluid bounds, the clamp max yields - cap fluidity lower or raise the max bound; user scaling never loses.

skills.name: Multilingual & Vietnamese Typography
skills.summary: Diacritic stacking, line-height headroom, fallback stacks, and locale conventions - first-class type for Vietnamese and other marked scripts.

sections.definition: Vietnamese and other diacritic-heavy scripts (Czech, Turkish, Indic) break typography that was designed for English only: stacked tone marks need line-height headroom, fonts need the right OpenType coverage (latin-ext, vietnamese subsets), and fallback stacks determine whether ề renders or becomes tofu. This skill makes marked-script typography a first-class constraint in family selection, scale, and rendering - not an afterthought discovered in QA.
principles: Vietnamese coverage is an adoption gate: fonts must include the vietnamese subset (Google Fonts flags it; foundries list it) - no coverage, no adoption.
Stacked marks need headroom: line-height >= 1.5 for body and >= 1.3 even for display - ề, ậ, ắ stack two marks vertically.
Subset your webfonts: ship latin + latin-ext + vietnamese subsets, not the monolithic file - load what the locale needs.
Fallback stacks follow the primary: every fallback in the stack must also carry Vietnamese coverage, or marks render from a different face (the 'mixed-face' look).
Uppercase transforms marks: Vietnamese caps carry full diacritics (À, Ạ) - do not strip them, and give caps extra tracking for the taller stack.
Locale conventions vary: Vietnamese uses no letter-spacing traditions; quotes, dashes, and number formatting follow the locale, not the source language.
Test real copy, not pangrams: 'Trăm năm trong cõi người ta' stresses different glyph pairs than 'The quick brown fox'.

tokens.notes: Required subsets per family; adoption gate
Display leading raised vs Latin 1.1 for mark clearance
unicode-range subsets; load only what renders
Real Vietnamese copy in QA, not pangrams
CJK taller leading; RTL no tracking (see letter-spacing)

composition: Composes with font-pairing: coverage is the first pairing gate - a beautiful face without the vietnamese subset is disqualified.
Composes with line-height: diacritic headroom can override Latin leading aesthetics at every scale step.
Composes with webfont-loading: subset strategy and unicode-range are the loading-side execution of coverage.
patterns: Mark-stress test page: a static page of worst-case Vietnamese strings (ộ, ế, ắ at every scale step and weight) screenshotted per release.
Fallback simulation: block the primary font in devtools; verify the fallback renders Vietnamese without metric jumps or tofu.
useCases: Products localizing into Vietnamese (the default audience for this skill set's authors).
Global products handling Czech, Turkish, Polish, Indic scripts with the same discipline.
Auditing: mixed-face diacritics, clipped marks, tofu glyphs in production.
antiPatterns: Tofu fallbacks: system stacks (Arial, Helvetica) missing Vietnamese where the custom font fails to load
Clipped display marks: hero headlines at 1.1 leading shearing tone marks
English-only QA: approving fonts from Latin-only test strings
Uppercase stripping: text-transform pipelines that drop Vietnamese diacritics (legacy encodings)

accessibility.notes: Clipped or tofu'd diacritics change meaning in Vietnamese (distinguishable words differ by marks) - legibility here is comprehension, not aesthetics: WCAG 1.4.4 zoom + marks headroom must hold together.
accessibility.fallback: If the primary face clips marks at a size, raise line-height for that step product-wide (see line-height tokens) - never switch faces per locale.

skills.name: Readability & Measure
skills.summary: Line length (45-75ch), contrast of reading surfaces, paragraph spacing, and the legibility properties that make long text effortless.

sections.definition: Readability is how effortlessly users process running text: line length (45-75 characters), comfortable leading, adequate contrast, and clean paragraphs. Legibility is the glyph-level property - open apertures, distinct letterforms, unambiguous 1/I/l. Together they decide whether users read the page or bounce from it; both are tokenizable (measure, leading, size) and both have WCAG floors (contrast 1.4.3, spacing 1.4.12).
principles: Measure 45-75ch, ideal ~66: longer lines lose the return path; shorter ones chop the reading rhythm.
Body size 16-18px minimum: below 16px, screen-distance reading degrades measurably - 14px is the floor for UI labels, not paragraphs.
Contrast of reading surfaces: body text passes 4.5:1 (AA) always; long-form reading surfaces target 7:1 (AAA).
Left-align, ragged right: justified text creates rivers and uneven word spacing; hyphenation needs care per language.
Paragraph rhythm: 1.5 leading + one blank line (or space-4) between paragraphs - spacing signals structure more than indenting.
Legibility check the letterforms: open apertures (a, e, c), tall x-height, distinct 1/l/I and O/0 - test at 14px where detail collapses first.
Reading width shrinks on zoom: at 200% zoom the 66ch paragraph reflows - the measure is in ch, so it self-adapts.

tokens.notes: The acceptable band; outside it, split columns
Measure adapts at zoom (ch scales with font)

composition: Composes with line-height and type-scale: measure + leading + size form the reading triangle - tune them together.
Composes with color-contrast (skill-accessibility guide 02): the 7:1 reading target is enforced on text aliases from skill-design-tokens.
It composes with accessible-typography: every readability floor is also an accessibility floor.
patterns: Reading component: one .prose class owns measure, leading, size, and spacing for articles - long-form text never styled ad hoc.
Glyph stress test: render 1lI O0 and dense paragraphs at 14px in QA; the face that fails here fails everywhere.
useCases: Documentation platforms and news sites (the 66ch measure is their spine).
Email readers and RSS clients where users read for minutes.
Audit: measuring actual rendered line lengths and paragraph spacing.
antiPatterns: Full-width paragraphs: 120ch lines that make eyes lose the return path
Tiny gray text: 13px #999 body that fails contrast and legibility simultaneously
Justified rivers: text-align: justify without hyphenation - uneven word gaps
Wall-of-text: no paragraph breaks, no headings, 2000-word blocks

accessibility.notes: This guide enforces the reading-side WCAG floors: 1.4.3 (contrast), 1.4.4 (zoom), 1.4.8 (visual presentation - measure, leading, justification), 1.4.12 (text spacing overrides).
accessibility.fallback: When a design needs a wider measure, split into columns (CSS columns) rather than stretching lines - the 75ch ceiling is a limit, not a suggestion.

skills.name: Webfont Loading & Performance
skills.summary: Fast, stable font delivery: subsets, font-display, preload discipline, and layout-shift prevention (CLS) that keeps text readable while fonts arrive.

sections.definition: Webfont loading is the performance contract of typography: fonts arrive fast (subsets, WOFF2, compression), text renders immediately (font-display swap), and layout does not jump when the real face lands (CLS). Every 100ms of font delay is perceived slowness; every reflow is user-visible jank. This skill covers the loading pipeline: what to load (subsets, weights), when to load (preload, swap), and how to fail (metric-matched fallbacks).
principles: WOFF2 only, subset per script: latin/latin-ext/vietnamese unicode-range subsets cut payload 50-80% versus monolithic files.
Load the closed weight set only: 2-3 weights per face (type tokens) - every extra weight is a request nobody needed.
font-display: swap with metric-matched fallbacks: text shows immediately in the fallback, swaps when ready - invisible-text periods (block) are worse than FOUT.
Preload only the primary subset: one <link rel=preload> for the above-the-fold body font; preloading everything delays everything.
Kill CLS with size-adjust: ascent-override/size-adjust on the fallback keeps layout stable while the real font loads.
Self-host when possible: third-party font CDNs add DNS/TLS round trips and privacy exposure; self-hosting wins on control.
Cache aggressively: immutable + max-age=31536000 on versioned font files - repeat visits cost zero.

tokens.notes: Modern browsers; no woff/ttf fallbacks needed
Text visible immediately in fallback face
Matches the closed type-token weight set

composition: Composes with font-pairing and variable-fonts: the closed weight set and subset strategy come from those decisions; loading executes them.
Composes with multilingual-vietnamese: unicode-range subsets are how Vietnamese coverage ships without payload bloat.
Composes with perceived-performance (skill-design-review guide 10): font loading is a top-3 source of layout shift and perceived slowness.
patterns: Self-hosted subset pipeline: build step subsets WOFF2 per script and emits @font-face with unicode-range + preload hints for the body font.
Fallback metric tuning: measure the primary face's ascent/size-adjust deltas once per family and bake them into the fallback declaration.
useCases: Any product loading custom fonts - the defaults here (swap + subsets + preload) are the starting config.
Performance audits: font payload, CLS from swaps, invisible-text periods.
Privacy-sensitive products: eliminating third-party font CDN exposure.
antiPatterns: Preload everything: six preloaded fonts starving the critical path
Block-then-render: font-display: block hiding text 3s behind an invisible period
Monolithic files: 400KB font files loading 6 weights and 3 scripts for one page
Third-party default: shipping Google Fonts CDN by default with no privacy/perf review

accessibility.notes: Loading strategy is an accessibility issue: invisible-text periods hide content from everyone (including screen readers mid-load), and CLS disorients users with motor or low-vision impairments most.
accessibility.fallback: If font loading cannot be optimized in time, system font stacks are a valid, fast, accessible default - custom fonts are an enhancement, never a dependency.

skills.name: Numeric & Tabular Figures
skills.summary: Proportional vs tabular figures, OpenType features, and data-typography: numbers that align in tables and count in dashboards.

sections.definition: Numeric typography is its own craft: tables need tabular (monospaced-width) figures so columns align; dashboards need them for count-ups and comparisons; prose needs proportional figures for natural rhythm. OpenType features (tnum, lnum, onum, zero, frac) decide which rendering a face produces - and default proportional figures in a data table is the classic misalignment nobody can name.
principles: Tables and dashboards get tnum: font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums on all numeric columns - digits share one width and align.
Prose keeps proportional figures: proportional digits read better in sentences; do not tnum the blog body.
Lining figures for data, oldstyle for editorial: lining (uniform height) suits tables and finance; oldstyle suits book typography.
Slashed or dotted zero for identifiers: font-variant-numeric: slashed-zero disambiguates O/0 in codes, tokens, and IDs.
Count-ups animate in tabular space: number animations (skill-animation data-animation) jitter unless digits are tabular-width.
Monospace for codes and tokens: IDs, hashes, and API keys use the mono token - copying accuracy beats aesthetics.
Currency and units outside the digits: '1,234,567 VND' - unit text uses the text face, digits keep tabular alignment.

tokens.notes: Dashboard KPIs: tabular + weight for stability
Units/currency in text face, digits tabular

composition: Composes with type-scale and font-pairing: figure features are declared per face - verify the chosen face supports tnum before adoption.
Composes with skill-component-recipes guide 03 (tables) and guide 12 (charts): tabular figures are a hard requirement in those recipes.
Composes with skill-animation data-animation: count-up choreography assumes tabular-width digits.
patterns: Data-typography utility: .num-table / .num-kpi classes bundle font-variant-numeric + face + size, so data UI consumes one class.
Feature support gate: family adoption checks tnum/zero coverage in the scorecard (font-pairing) - a data-product face without tnum is disqualified.
useCases: Financial dashboards and tables where column alignment is trust.
Analytics products with animated KPI count-ups.
Developer tools rendering IDs, hashes, and config values.
antiPatterns: Proportional tables: default figures in data columns - columns shimmer with misalignment
Jittering count-ups: animated numbers without tabular-nums twitching on every frame
tnum everywhere: tabular figures in prose making sentences stiff
Ambiguous zeros: O/0 confusion in rendered IDs where slashed-zero cost nothing

accessibility.notes: Aligned numeric columns are a comprehension aid for dyslexic and low-vision users; slashed-zero removes transcription errors - data typography is cognitive accessibility in disguise.
accessibility.fallback: If the face lacks OpenType numeric features, switch data surfaces to the mono face - mono digits are tabular by construction.

skills.name: Variable Fonts
skills.summary: One file, many styles: weight/optical axes, named instances, and when a variable font beats static weights - plus the loading math.

sections.definition: Variable fonts encode an entire design space (weight, width, optical size, slant) in one file along continuous axes: font-variation-settings or high-level properties (font-weight, font-optical-sizing) pick any point. The payoff: one 60-90KB file replaces 3-5 static weights, enables fine-grained hierarchy (weight 550), and unlocks optical sizing. The cost: axis abuse ( animating weight on text ) and fallback complexity.
principles: Adopt when axes exceed static needs: 3+ weights or optical sizing justifies one variable file; 2 weights may be cheaper static.
High-level properties first: font-weight/font-stretch/font-optical-sizing map to axes and inherit correctly - font-variation-settings is a low-level escape hatch.
Named instances are the safe menu: expose axis values as named tokens (400/600/700), not raw axis playgrounds.
Optical size axes are free micro-typography: font-optical-sizing: auto selects display/text cuts at every size - better tracking and contrast for free.
Do not animate weight on reading text: weight interpolation on body text reflows lines every frame (layout shift + unreadable) - animate color/opacity instead.
One variable file per family: loading a variable font AND its static weights doubles cost - pick one strategy per face.
Fallback metrics still apply: variable or not, fallbacks need size-adjust tuning (see webfont-loading).

tokens.notes: Variable replaces static weights; never both
wght axis range as loaded (subset if narrower)
font-optical-sizing: auto when opsz axis exists
The tokenized subset users may pick
Custom axes (slnt, GRAD) need design review
Weight animation on reading text forbidden
GRAD axes for subtle emphasis, not hierarchy
Variable fonts have universal modern support

composition: Composes with type-scale: named instance tokens plug into the scale's text roles - weight 600 at 25px is one role definition.
Composes with webfont-loading: one variable file simplifies the loading pipeline (fewer requests, same subsets).
Composes with skill-design-tokens guide 02: the weight budget in tokens maps to the variable axis range.
patterns: Tokenized instances: font-weight tokens (400/600/700) expose only reviewed axis points; raw axis values fail lint.
Optical-first display: for families with opsz, let optical sizing handle display/text cuts instead of separate files.
useCases: Products needing rich hierarchy (many weights) without payload multiplication.
Editorial/display-heavy products benefiting from optical sizing.
Reducing font requests in performance-critical apps.
antiPatterns: Double loading: variable file + static weights shipped together
Axis playground: unreviewed wght values (537) appearing wherever a developer felt like it
Weight-animated paragraphs: body text morphing weight and reflowing every frame
Max-range files: loading wght 100-900 when the product uses 3 instances

accessibility.notes: Named instances protect predictability: screen magnifier and low-vision users rely on consistent weights; weight animation on text also violates reduced-motion norms (perpetual motion).
accessibility.fallback: If variable font behavior is unpredictable in a target browser, fall back to static weights of the same family - identical tokens, different delivery.

skills.name: Accessible Typography
skills.summary: The a11y floors for text: contrast, zoom, spacing overrides, dyslexia-friendly defaults, and semantic structure that AT can navigate.

sections.definition: Accessible typography is the set of floors every text surface must clear: 4.5:1 contrast (7:1 for long-form), rem-based sizes that honor 200% zoom, respect for user text-spacing overrides (WCAG 1.4.12), real heading structure for screen reader navigation, and letterform choices that reduce reading errors for dyslexic users. Text is the majority of most interfaces - typography is therefore the majority of accessibility.
principles: Contrast floors are absolute: 4.5:1 body, 7:1 long-form targets - no aesthetic override (pairs with a11y repo color-contrast).
Sizes in rem, zoom-proof: all type tokens are rem; 200% zoom must leave every control functional (1.4.4).
Respect user spacing overrides: layouts must survive users setting line-height 1.5x, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em (1.4.12).
Real headings, real structure: h1-h6 outline matches the visual hierarchy; screen readers navigate by headings - divs styled as headings are a bug.
Links distinguish themselves: underline + color (or ≥2 signals) - color alone fails 1.4.1 and users with color vision deficiency.
Dyslexia-friendly defaults: generous leading (1.5+), left alignment, longer line spacing between paragraphs, uncluttered backgrounds.
No text in images of text: real text scales, translates, and reflows (1.4.5) - images-of-text only for logos/essential.
Reading overrides beat brand aesthetics: if 1.4.12 overrides break the layout, the layout is too rigid - fix the layout.

tokens.notes: All flows pass at 200% text zoom

composition: Composes with skill-accessibility: color-contrast, zoom-reflow, and cognitive-content are the specialized guides behind these floors.
Composes with skill-design-tokens guide 02: type tokens carry the rem/contrast guarantees; this guide states the a11y rationale.
Composes with readability-legibility: readability floors and a11y floors are the same numbers viewed from two sides.
patterns: Override-stress test: apply the 1.4.12 spacing overrides in devtools; any broken layout becomes a bug with the screenshot attached.
Heading lint: CI checks one h1, ordered h-levels, and no styled-div headings per page.
useCases: Any text-heavy product claiming WCAG AA.
Dyslexia-inclusive products (education, reading, government).
Audit: contrast, zoom, spacing-override, and heading-structure passes.
antiPatterns: Outline:none on text: removing focus indication from links and inputs
Gray-on-white hierarchy: de-ranking text below 4.5:1 instead of using weight/size
Div headings: styled divs where screen readers need h1-h6
Rigid layouts: designs that shatter when users apply legal spacing overrides

accessibility.notes: This guide IS the accessibility layer of typography: every floor cited (1.4.3, 1.4.4, 1.4.5, 1.4.8, 1.4.12) is a conformance criterion, and heading structure is the screen reader's primary navigation.
accessibility.fallback: When brand type choices conflict with floors, floors win - the brand adjusts (darker shade, larger size), never the criterion.
